opening.headline: Learn the principles of preference optimization and data formats that teach models through comparison when there is no single correct answer and only a better answer can be identified.
body: Although it is easy to tell which of two answers is better, it is often difficult to write a perfect model answer yourself. This is especially true for criteria such as tone, focus of the summary, and brevity.

In this lesson, we will look at data formats and settings for DPO to tune a model with pairs of selected and rejected responses. The process of changing the tone, the process of learning criteria for which there is no model answer, and the selection criteria for SFT are summarized.

screens.title: There is a better answer, but there is no standard answer.
screens.lead:
Compare and read two answers to the same question. Think about which is better and whether you can come up with one perfect answer.

visual.alt: A scene showing two answer cards A and B side by side to the same question.
labels: Please tell me the weather in Seoul tomorrow
Tomorrow, Seoul will be cloudy in the morning and then clear, and the highest temperature will be around 20 degrees.

paragraphs: A user asked, ‘Tell me the weather in Seoul tomorrow.’ Answer A is 'The weather is not bad.' Answer B is a response containing flow and specific temperature by time zone. When it comes to which is better, most people give the same answer.

However, when asked to write down the ideal response in one sentence, each person writes it differently. This is because it is all up to you to decide what temperature to use, how to speak, and how long to write. It's easy to compare, but it's hard to write a single best example output.

OpenAI's Preferred Optimization document describes DPO finetuning with prompt and response pairs for these situations. This method learns people's preferences, which are more subjective, and optimizes the model to produce output that is more likely to be preferred. This class covers the principles and data of DPO and its differences from SFT.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What criteria make it easier to compare two answers than to write down the correct answer? Check out examples in class.

screens.outro: Let's think about whether there are cases in your work where comparison is easy, but writing directly is difficult.

screens.title: Think of cases where it is easy to compare but difficult to write directly.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there times when you can say which of two answers is better, but find it difficult to write a model answer?
items.answer: Examples include tasks where there is more than one good outcome, such as summaries, customer service copy, and promotional copy. In these tasks, comparative judgment is easier and faster than writing.

items.prompt: Is it tone or focus of the summary?
items.answer: OpenAI documents are suitable for DPOs to summarize text with a focus on key points and create conversational messages with the right tone and style. Tone and focus of the summary are representative standards for teaching by comparison.

items.prompt: Are the standards organized in writing?
items.answer: If the criteria are not written down, different people will choose different sides, creating contradictions in preference data. In this lesson, we will see why consistency of standards is a prerequisite for learning.

screens.outro: Now that we've got our thoughts together, let's take a look at what our preference pairs data looks like and is set up.

screens.title: Setting up preferred pair data and DPO tasks
screens.lead: The code below is an example preference pair and a call to create a DPO tuning operation. Check the meaning of each field and setting in the explanation on the right.

notes.note: The input is a user message. According to the OpenAI documentation, it currently only trains for single-turn conversations, so preferred and unpreferred messages must be the last Assistant message in the conversation.

preferred_output is the ideal response and non_preferred_output is the less desirable response. The two responses must be for the same input for the comparison to be meaningful. When standards are applied differently from person to person, the direction of the pairs is reversed and learning becomes blurred.
Data is stored in JSONL format, one example per line. One line is a pair.

When creating a task, specify the method type as dpo and set hyperparameters if necessary. Beta is a value between 0 and 2, where larger means more likely to maintain previous behavior and smaller means more actively follows new preferences. If set to auto, the value determined by the platform is used.

screens.outro: Now that we have the data format in place, let's compare how the tone changes as preference pairs stack up.

screens.title: The process of tone change in preferred pairs
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the responses before and after learning. Notice what the model reinforces.

visual.alt: Schematic showing a shift in the model's output distribution toward a choice response.

states.label: Before learning
states.body:
**Request**: User asks ‘Tell me the weather in Seoul tomorrow.’

**Response**: The base model sometimes says 'the weather isn't that bad.' Mix the same short, vague responses with information-rich responses. It is difficult to predict what the response will be.

**Limitations to Prompts**: You can instruct someone to write a specific temperature, but subtle preferences such as tone, length, and balance of information are difficult to write down as instructions. In this state, the starting point for learning is to create an evaluation question and set criteria for which response is preferred. It is easy to compare changes after learning by asking the same question multiple times to see how the responses fluctuate.

states.label: After learning
states.body:
**Learning**: Preference pairs are stacked for the same question, with information-rich responses recorded as choices and ambiguous responses recorded as rejections. The model strengthens patterns that are closer to choice responses and weakens patterns that are closer to rejection responses.

**Results**: Trained models more often respond to the same questions with specific temperature and flow information. Rather than imitating the only exemplary output, you learn which direction is better.

**Best Uses**: OpenAI documents create summaries that focus on the point, and messages with the right tone and style. This method is suitable for reflecting subjective human preferences.

**Premise**: The preference criteria must be consistent for the pair to make sense. As the standard fluctuates from pair to pair, the direction in which the model will learn also fluctuates.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the teaching method through comparison, let us explain the procedure for learning standards for which there is no model answer.

screens.title: Explanation: Learning criteria for which there is no model answer, such as ‘succinct answer’
screens.lead: The instructor explains a team's case step by step, from setting standards to evaluating. Select the right arrow to skip a step. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Situation: The answer is too long
steps.body: One team of chatbots gives accurate answers, but always speaks at length. Users want more concise answers. There is no single right answer when it comes to brevity. Sometimes one sentence is good, sometimes two sentences are good.

steps.title: Step 1: Set standards in writing
steps.body: First, write down the criteria in detail. For example, if you write something like, ‘Keep the main points in one or two sentences and omit any background explanations that the user didn’t ask for,’ there will be less difference in judgment between people. If the standards are not written down, all subsequent steps will be shaky. For example, itemizing the upper limit on the length of responses, the extent of background information allowed, and key information that must be left out ensures that the people creating the pair can read and judge against the same criteria.

steps.title: Step 2: Create pairs of responses to the same question
steps.body: For the same question, record a concise response as a choice and a lengthy response as a rejection. Both responses must match. If one side is wrong, the pair ends up comparing accuracy rather than brevity. For example, check each pair to see if the choice response is concise but doesn't leave out key figures, or if the rejection response is just longer but has the same content.

steps.title: Step 3: Multiple people create to the same standard
steps.body: If a pair is created by multiple people, they must follow the same standards document. The OpenAI documentation explains that when tuning data in general is created by multiple people, the degree of agreement between people can limit performance. This principle also applies to preference data.

steps.title: Step 4: Adhere to data quality principles
steps.body: Balance, diversity, and uniformity of form must also be maintained. If the reject response is always long and the select response is always short, the model can only learn length. Organize question types to match your operational environment.

steps.title: Step 5: Learn and check with evaluation set
steps.body: After determining beta and training, check it with an evaluation set that was not used for training. Just looking at it for simplicity is not enough. We need to see whether brevity and accuracy are maintained together. If accuracy is poor, adjust the pair composition or beta. At this time, the object of comparison is the response of the pre-trained model to the same evaluation question.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: Even standards with no correct answer can be learned through the process of written standards, consistent pairs, balanced data, and evaluation. Even in the comparative teaching method, consistency of standards is the most important premise. In practice, the four stages of standard document creation, pair composition inspection, learning, and evaluation are viewed as one iterative cycle, and if the results do not meet expectations, the standard document is read again.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the process, let's finally compare how to choose between SFT and DPO.

screens.title: Should I use SFT or DPO?
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the data, intended uses, and limitations of both methods.

tabs.label: SFT
tabs.body:
**Data**: A pair of prompts and desired model output. It can only be created if there is a unique exemplary output.

**Good for**: Tasks where the correct answer is obvious, such as classification, creating content in a specific format, or correcting failure to follow instructions. For format fixation, SFT is natural.

**Limitations**: Standards that do not have a single correct answer make it difficult to create data because it is difficult to write exemplary output.

**Selection Question**: First, ask whether the correct output for this task can be written down in one way. If you can write it down, SFT is the candidate. It's difficult to write down, but if you can choose between the two responses, DPO is the candidate.

tabs.label: DPO
tabs.body:
**Data**: Prompts and responses selected and rejected. If you can compare which one is better, you can make it.

**Benefits**: Tasks that reflect subjective preferences, such as focused summaries and creating messages with the right tone and style.

**Limitation**: If preference criteria are inconsistent, the pair loses meaning. Accuracy does not automatically increase with preferred learning and must be checked separately through evaluation.

**Common Preparation**: Both methods require you to first establish a baseline of assessments and prompts.

**Choice question**: Asks whether people can consistently choose which of two responses is better. If you can't choose consistently, you should first overhaul your baseline documents.

screens.outro: I will summarize today's highlights in the last screen.

screens.title: Preference Optimization is Taught by Comparison
screens.lead: We organize by answering the first question: how to teach when there is a better answer but no standard answer.

paragraphs: Standards that cannot determine a single correct answer are taught through comparison. DPO's data are pairs of choice and rejection responses to the same prompt, and the model reinforces patterns that approximate choice responses. This approach suits subjective preferences such as tone, focus of the summary, and brevity.

If there is a unique exemplary output and the goal is to fix the format, SFT is natural, and if only good and bad comparisons are possible, DPO is natural. Either way, first establish a baseline of assessments and prompts.

Lastly, remember to be consistent in your standards. Data only becomes meaningful when the criteria are written down and multiple people create pairs based on the same criteria. After training, we use an evaluation set to check whether the targeted features and accuracy are maintained together. Only after this inspection is completed can the learned model be used for operation.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: If you can write a model answer, you are SFT, and if you can only choose the better answer, you are DPO.

glossary.def: This is a training example that groups selected and rejected responses to the same prompt.
It stands for Direct Preference Optimization, and is a method of tuning a model to produce more preferred output using a pair of prompts and responses.
A value between 0 and 2 in DPO that controls how much of the previous behavior is maintained. The bigger the more conservative.
This field contains the ideal response from the preferred pair.
This field contains the less appropriate response from the preferred pair.

misconceptions.myth: DPO is upward compatible with SFT.
misconceptions.fact: The two methods have different data and uses. If there is a model output, SFT is natural, and if only comparison is possible, DPO is natural.

misconceptions.myth: Preference pairs can be created in any way.
misconceptions.fact: Learning is only meaningful when standards are consistent. When the reference wavers, the direction of the pair also wavers.

misconceptions.myth: If you learn preference, accuracy automatically increases.
misconceptions.fact: Accuracy must be separately verified. Check with the evaluation set to ensure that accuracy does not decrease as tone or brevity changes.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Preference optimization is taught by comparison.
The basis of the data is a pair of prompts and selected and rejected responses.
DPO is suitable for tone and quality preferences, and SFT is suitable for format fixation with unique exemplary output.
Data only has meaning if the standards are consistent.
